opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those questions where I think it's useful to start from the most extreme reference points and work inward.

On one end, you've got biology. Fruit flies can double their population in something like a week or two. Some bacteria double in twenty minutes. Those are self-replicating systems built from atoms, running on sunlight and chemistry, and they show you that physics doesn't forbid really fast replication. So the hard floor is clearly way below anything our current economy does.

On the other end, you've got the human economy, which doubles every twenty or thirty years. But almost none of that is a physical limit. It's mostly that the economy is bottlenecked on humans: how fast we can train people, how fast we grow the population, how slowly organizations coordinate and learn. Factories aren't running flat out all the time trying to build more factories. Most output goes to consumption.

So the question is: suppose you remove the human bottleneck. You've got superintelligent AI designing things and running the show, and robots doing the physical work. How fast could that whole system double?

One way I like to think about it is to ask how long it takes a factory, or a set of factories plus mines plus power plants, to produce an equivalent of itself. If you look at something like a modern car factory, it produces cars whose total mass and value is comparable to the factory itself on a timescale of maybe a year or less. If you redirect that kind of capacity toward building robots and more factories, and you have AI that is better at optimizing everything, it seems plausible you could get doubling times of months, maybe faster.

And then there's the question of how far down you could push it with better design. If superintelligences come up with much more efficient manufacturing, maybe closer to what biology does, you could imagine doubling times of weeks. I'd hold that more loosely, because the frontier there depends on technologies we don't have yet.

What are the real constraints? Energy is a big one. Eventually you're limited by how much power you can generate, and building power plants takes time too, though solar is pretty fast to deploy and getting faster. Raw materials and mining matter. Heat dissipation matters at very large scales. There's also a learning-by-doing aspect: even superintelligences need to run experiments in the physical world, and some of those have irreducible wall-clock time, like waiting for a chemical process or testing how something wears over time.

But my overall take is that none of those seem to impose a limit anywhere near the current twenty-year doubling. I think a fully automated robot economy could plausibly double in a year or less fairly quickly after it gets going, and then potentially accelerate from there toward much shorter times. I'd put a lot of uncertainty on the exact numbers. The basic point is that the physical ceiling is very far above where we are now, and the main reason we don't grow faster today is us, not physics.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fruit flies and bacteria as examples of fast biological replication and separately says robot-economy doubling in weeks is conceivable. It does not use grass doubling within weeks as evidence.

r002.rationale: The response discusses possible doubling times of months, weeks, and a year or less, but does not suggest doubling in a few hours.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair amount, and I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows, but we can at least bound it. The way I'd frame it is: what's the doubling time of a fully automated economy — robots building robots, factories building factories — once you take humans out of the loop entirely?

The reference class I find most useful is biology. A fruit fly or a bacterium is basically a self-replicating machine, and bacteria can double in something like twenty minutes to an hour. Larger organisms take longer — a rabbit population can double in months, humans take decades — but the point is that nature has already demonstrated self-replicating systems with doubling times measured in hours to weeks, not years. That's an existence proof that the physics allows it. Whether human-designed robotics can get anywhere near that is a separate question, but it tells you the ceiling isn't where people's intuitions put it.

Then on the other end, you can look at the current industrial economy. Right now a car factory takes a couple of years to build, and the global economy doubles every twenty-five years or so. But a lot of that is bottlenecked on things that go away if you have superintelligent AI and full automation — permitting, labor, coordination failures, the fact that humans need to sleep and eat and be trained. Tesla or the Chinese EV companies have shown you can stand up a gigafactory in under a year when you're really motivated. So even with today's technology and just much better management, I think you could plausibly get to doubling times of a year or so.

Where I actually land is something like: once you have the robots-building-robots loop going, and you have superintelligence doing the engineering and the R&D, I'd guess doubling times on the order of months to a year are quite plausible within a few years of that transition. And it's not crazy that it goes faster than that, down to weeks, as the designs get optimized for replication speed specifically rather than for whatever we currently optimize for.

The hard physical constraints I'd point to are things like energy — you need to be producing solar panels or whatever faster than you're consuming power — raw material extraction and refining, and just the latency of physical processes. Concrete takes time to cure, you can't move mass around instantaneously, chemical reactions have rates. Those put a floor on it. But I think when people say "the physical world is slow," they're often just importing the speed of the current human economy, which is slow for reasons that mostly aren't physics.

So my central guess is a doubling time of under a year, with real uncertainty in both directions, and I think the thing that matters strategically is that even the conservative end of that range is a completely different world from the one we live in now.

r001.rationale: The response cites bacteria doubling in minutes to an hour and other biological examples, but it does not mention grass or use grass doubling within weeks as evidence for robot-economy doubling within weeks.

r002.rationale: It says robot-economy doubling in weeks is not crazy, but does not suggest doubling in a few hours; the few-hour timescale applies only to bacteria.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between how fast you can make the robots and how fast you can expand the whole industrial system that makes the robots. A robot might be assembled quite quickly, but that doesn’t mean the economy can double that quickly. You also need more mines, refineries, power plants, chip factories, and transportation capacity.

One way to think about it is: suppose you have a whole industrial system that’s autonomous, including the production of its own replacement parts. How long would it take that system to build another system like itself? That’s the doubling time we’re interested in. And it depends on the bottlenecks along that entire chain, rather than just on how intelligent the software is.

Intelligence could help a lot. You could redesign factories for rapid construction, run experiments in parallel, and find substitutes for materials or processes that are slowing you down. But you still have to move matter around, supply energy, and wait for physical processes to happen.

So I don’t have a confident number for the physical limit. I think doubling times much shorter than those of the human economy are plausible. But going from that to, say, doubling every week requires a concrete account of how the entire supply chain expands that quickly. You can’t infer it just from the fact that an AI can copy itself in seconds.

r001.rationale: The response does not use grass doubling within weeks as evidence; it says weekly doubling would require a concrete account of the supply chain.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest doubling in a few hours. It says physical doubling depends on industrial bottlenecks and rejects inferring it from AI copying itself in seconds.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between how fast you can copy the intelligence and how fast you can build the physical machinery. If you have a capable AI, you might be able to make more copies of it quite quickly, provided you have the chips. But making more chips, robots, power plants, and factories requires moving atoms around, and that’s where the harder constraints come in.

The relevant question is something like: how long does it take an entire industrial system to produce another industrial system of comparable productive capacity? You can’t just look at how quickly a robot can assemble another robot, because you also need to account for the mines, the refineries, the machine tools, and so on.

I don’t have a confident estimate of the minimum doubling time. I could imagine it being much shorter than we’re used to—months, perhaps—but I wouldn’t treat that as an established physical limit. Some industrial processes take time, and you’d have to work out which can be accelerated, which can be replaced, and which remain bottlenecks.

And there’s an important distinction between the initial transition and the eventual limit. Initially, you’re working with existing factories and supply chains. Later, you might have a system designed from the ground up for rapid expansion. So even if the first doubling takes quite a while, that doesn’t tell you how fast subsequent doublings could be.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a possible doubling time of months and discusses industrial bottlenecks, but it does not use grass doubling within weeks as evidence or claim physical doubling within weeks.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest doubling in a few hours; it offers months as a speculative possibility and says it lacks a confident minimum-time estimate.
